clue.text: French teacher produced wine, around one

indicators.note: the wine goes around the one, holding it inside

explanation.surface: A French teacher who makes wine on the side, with a glass or two going around.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools the French teacher, if female, was traditionally addressed as Mademoiselle, so the title stands for the teacher. The one sits inside the wine: MO(I)SELLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils in British schools called a female French teacher Mademoiselle, so the title names the teacher.

clue.text: Evangelist taking part in scam at the weekend

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A preacher caught up in some weekend swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across four words, starting at the end of 'scam' and finishing on the first letter of 'weekend'.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew is one of the four Evangelists, the writers of the Gospels.

clue.text: Two head out with toddler sound asleep

indicators.note: letters that are out are disordered, as in 'put out'

explanation.surface: Two parents head out for the evening, leaving the toddler fast asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' reads as going out for the night, but it tells you to rearrange the letters of 'two head' and 'toddler' together.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dead to the world is so deeply asleep that nothing wakes them.

clue.text: Artist Norway greatly takes to heart

indicators.note: the word for greatly holds the other letter in its middle

parts.note: N is the international code for Norway

explanation.surface: A Norwegian artist beloved by his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: Edvard Munch, painter of The Scream, was Norwegian, so the surface is true to life.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Munch was the Norwegian painter of The Scream.

clue.text: Sovereign put in danger keeps close to Camilla

indicators.note: the word for put in danger holds the letter inside it
the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A monarch endangered, holding Camilla close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sovereign' is an adjective here, as in sovereign power, matching IMPERIAL. The A goes in before the final L of IMPERIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial means belonging to an emperor or supreme ruler, which is what sovereign means as an adjective.

clue.text: Gets down from saddle after cycling

indicators.note: letters cycle round: the first moves to the end

parts.note: a saddle is a seat; S moves from front to back

explanation.surface: A cyclist dismounting after a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets down' looks like dismounting from a bicycle, but it means swallows food. 'Cycling' sits naturally beside 'saddle' while telling you to rotate SEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To get food down is to swallow it, so gets down means eats.

clue.text: Smell's back, is anyone cooking with onions?

indicators.note: letters being cooked are mixed up
the back of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs the air and asks whether anybody is frying onions.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides at the end as a phrase, 'with onions', rather than a noun: lyonnaise describes a dish cooked that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyonnaise, in the style of Lyon, is the menu term for food cooked with onions.

clue.text: Henry punches unattractive clown behind dark bar

indicators.note: the letter punches its way into the clown
the last piece comes behind the rest

parts.note: Coco the Clown, a famous circus clown
H = henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Someone called Henry lands a punch on an ugly clown behind a shady pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark bar' reads as a gloomy pub but is a bar of chocolate. 'Behind' does double duty as a word, LATE, rather than a position instruction. Coco the Clown was a famous British circus clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain chocolate is the British name for dark chocolate, sold in bars.

clue.text: Greek bronze found after sailors docked

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the last letter goes
the bronze comes after the sailors

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek bronze turns up where sailors have moored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' belongs with sailors and ships, but here it means cut short, taking the W off CREW. 'Bronze' is a suntan, not a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Crete is a Greek island, so a Cretan is a Greek named by one particular birthplace.

clue.text: School pictures brought back home

indicators.note: the word is brought back to front

explanation.surface: School paintings carried back to the house at the end of term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is a verb here, to teach, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: schooling a horse or a pupil means drilling it until it has learnt.

clue.text: Post office worker admits second-rate, shoddy work

indicators.note: the worker lets the letter in

explanation.surface: A postal worker confesses his job is poor and sloppy.
explanation.walkthrough: A potboiler is a book or painting churned out to pay the bills, keeping the pot boiling.
explanation.definitionFit: A potboiler is hack work produced quickly for money, so shoddy work.

clue.text: Arch they converted to a fish delivery business

indicators.note: converted letters are changed into a new form

explanation.surface: A railway arch turned into premises for a fishmonger's delivery firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: a 'fish delivery business' sounds like a van service, but the delivery is birth, fish hatching from eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchery is where fish eggs are hatched, a business delivering young fish into the world.

clue.text: A little oregano in the oil

indicators.note: only a little of the words is taken, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: add a pinch of oregano to the oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil' is a verb here: to anoint is to smear with oil, as in a ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: To anoint someone is to oil them, usually as a religious rite.

clue.text: Scratch using pencil

parts.note: with = using, as in 'written with a pen'

explanation.surface: Making a mark with a pencil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratch' and 'pencil' both suggest marks on paper, but scratch means to pull out of a race or contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To scratch a horse or competitor is to withdraw it from the event.

clue.text: Wavy dippy seas troubled tummy

indicators.note: wavy letters are not in a straight line, so out of order

explanation.surface: Choppy, rolling seas bringing on seasickness.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is seasickness, which fits the answer neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical word for indigestion, which the definition describes informally as an upset stomach.

clue.text: Show Tory how to be cool

parts.note: to air something is to show it

explanation.surface: Advice to a Conservative politician on looking hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' reads as fashionable, but it means kept at a low temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Air-con, air conditioning, is how a room or car is kept cool.

clue.text: Pose painter set up to test skills

definitions.note: plural skills defines the uncountable noun artistry

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means written upwards, so reversed

parts.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: An artist arranges a sitter as a way of testing their abilities.
explanation.walkthrough: The painter is not the obvious ARTIST: a Royal Academician is the crossword painter. In a down clue 'set up' means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The craft of an artist; the plural stands for the whole range of such abilities.

clue.text: Leading couple in play given moderate cheer

indicators.note: the first two letters of the word

explanation.surface: The lead actors in a play get only lukewarm applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading couple' sounds like the stars of the play, but it takes the first two letters. 'Cheer' is a verb meaning gladden.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean making someone glad.

clue.text: Father forces open boot, at last

indicators.note: only the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Dad jemmies the car boot open in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' is the title of a Catholic priest, not a parent. A boot here is the British word for a car's trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic priests are addressed as Father.

clue.text: The one time to regret nothing

explanation.surface: A motto: the one moment you must not rue anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The one' reads as 'the only', but it is a noun: the person you are destined for.
explanation.definitionFit: Your true love is 'the one', the person meant for you.

clue.text: Square English archdeacon with no secret desires

parts.note: someone who is out no longer hides their sexuality

explanation.surface: A strait-laced English churchman with nothing to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like an adjective meaning prim, which suits the churchman, but it is a verb, to level. An archdeacon is styled 'the Venerable'.
explanation.definitionFit: To square things is to even them out, making them level.

clue.text: Irish drink, dead smooth

definitions.note: adjective smooth for past participle ironed

parts.note: a drink is 'one', as in 'fancy one?'

explanation.surface: An Irish whiskey that goes down very smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' pairs with drink in the surface, but it defines a pressed shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Past participle of the household chore: a pressed shirt has had its creases flattened.

clue.text: Cornice excited English tour guide

indicators.note: excited letters are agitated into a new order

explanation.surface: An English guide gets carried away pointing out an ornate cornice.
explanation.walkthrough: A cicerone is an old word for a guide who explains antiquities to sightseers, named after the orator Cicero.
explanation.definitionFit: A cicerone is a guide who shows tourists the sights.

clue.text: One at the top in English literature

definitions.text: One at the top in English literature

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter
that letter goes inside the literature

explanation.surface: A tribute to a great of English letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes T. S. Eliot (or George Eliot) while the wordplay puts one inside E LIT.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot and George Eliot both stand at the top of English literature.

clue.text: A Christmas Carol's a heartless book

indicators.note: the middle letter is taken out

parts.note: front of NOVEL once its central V is gone
back of NOVEL after the V

explanation.surface: A verdict that Dickens's A Christmas Carol is a soulless book.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it look like Dickens's novel, but the definition is literal: a Christmas carol, which is a noel. Dickens's story really is a book, so the surface plays on that.
explanation.definitionFit: From the French word for Christmas, noel names a song sung at that season, so the book title works as a plain description.

clue.text: Make too little of magic drink, wanting the power to vanish?

indicators.note: the word is missing something
something that vanishes is no longer there, so the letter drops out of the word

parts.note: a short is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A wizard's potion that loses its strength and fails to make anyone disappear.
explanation.walkthrough: The SPELL loses its P before the drink joins. A 'short' is British for a single measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell something short is to undervalue it, making too little of it.

clue.text: After halfway, swim back, butterfly?

indicators.note: take only what comes after the midpoint of the word

explanation.surface: A swimmer turning halfway through a butterfly race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butterfly' looks like the swimming stroke, but it is the insect; the question mark flags it as an example of an imago.
explanation.definitionFit: An imago is the adult stage of an insect, and a butterfly is one example.

clue.text: Realty there's for doctoring

indicators.note: doctored letters have been tampered with

explanation.surface: A property note: the buildings there are used for medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: Harley Street is a London street famous for private doctors' practices, so the whole clue describes it while 'doctoring' also scrambles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Harley Street in London is real estate given over to doctors' consulting rooms.
